units.text: ‘It is not my decision. That is how the world works.’ Few formulas can move responsibility so quickly. Sometimes the speaker correctly warns us of a constraint. At other times they try to turn a contestable choice into an inevitability.

There is no single class of people benefiting from the concept of a law of nature. A reproducible result can protect a vulnerable person from arbitrariness and give a powerful organization a new instrument of control. The same physical principle can make a device safer or a weapon more effective. The distribution of benefits depends on access, aims and institutions, not merely the law’s truth.

The first gain is reduced dependence on the authority’s person. If we can show how a result is obtained and under what conditions, competence can be transmitted. A student need not inherit a teacher’s prestige to verify a calculation. This is the ideal. Realizing it nevertheless requires instruments, time, education and freedom to contradict, all unequally distributed.

The sociology of science shows why declared universality of criteria does not automatically eliminate hierarchies of recognition. Merton analyzed the ‘Matthew effect’: contributions associated with already prestigious researchers may receive disproportionate credit, while similar contributions from lesser-known researchers remain less visible. His analysis concerns recognition mechanisms, not proof that scientific results are merely products of reputation (Merton, 1968) .

The distinction is crucial. The social origin of trust does not automatically establish the truth or falsity of its object. It may explain why a correct idea is ignored or a weak one receives more attention. Evaluation also requires content, replication and independent results.

Nosek, Spies and Motyl discuss the tension between incentives for publishable results and incentives for accuracy. Favoring novelty and positive results can affect analytical choices and the visibility of negative findings. Their proposals concern research practices and rewards. Here we see that trust in laws is supported not only by intelligent minds but also by institutions making correction advantageous (Nosek, Spies și Motyl, 2012) .

The second gain is anticipatory power. Whoever knows a regularity before others can design, prevent or exploit. This asymmetry is not inherently illegitimate: competence is valuable. It becomes problematic when affected people cannot see assumptions, contest errors or negotiate consequences.

Imagine a model estimating a person’s probability of dropping out of a training program. The organization uses it to deny access to those deemed ‘risks’. The denial may prevent precisely the experience that would have changed the outcome. Prediction becomes part of the mechanism. We no longer merely observe a relationship: we use it to modify the world in which it was measured. The example is hypothetical, but shows why a social regularity cannot automatically be treated as a planetary orbit.

The third gain is legitimacy. When a hierarchy is called natural, its opponent seems to fight reality rather than an institution. We must decompose the claim: there is an observed difference; there is an explanation of causes; there is a judgment about what should be done. The first alone does not yield the second, and the first two do not automatically yield the third.

Saying a result has a biological component does not establish what moral treatment the person deserves. Saying a social measure has costs does not establish that it is unjustified. Saying an ideal is good does not prove the proposed mechanism will realize it. Rigor demands that facts, causes and values remain distinct, then enter explicit dialogue.

Who loses when the notion is misused? The person turned into a statistical average, the community told change is impossible and the researcher whose results do not fit the dominant story. Who loses when we reject the notion altogether? Those who depend on verifiable standards for safety, fair access and challenging arbitrariness.

The alternative is not between obedience to experts and distrust of all expertise. It is an organization of trust in which competence has authority within its domain while decision-making power remains accountable for values, distribution and errors. Nature does not vote on the budget or decide who deserves to suffer. Humans make these choices, sometimes using knowledge of nature, sometimes hiding behind it.
